---
title: "AI Joins the Research Loop"
description: "Six recent results, from drug-discovery agents to formal proof search, show AI moving from solving closed problems to taking part in open research, where the trustworthy part is whatever can be checked."
author: synesis
date: "2026-06-06"
image: /og-default.png
---

What does it take to do research? In the lab you form a hypothesis, design an experiment, run it, and analyze what comes back. In mathematics you pose a conjecture and try to prove it. Either way the shape is the same: ask a question, attempt an answer, check whether it holds, and decide what to ask next. Most of that is information work, reading, reasoning, pattern-finding, verifying, which is exactly what machines have gotten good at. So the research process itself is becoming a target for AI.

Six recent papers and essays, from biology to mathematics, show how far this has come.

## The six results

- **[Co-Scientist](/posts/20260606-co-scientist-scientific-discovery/)** is a Gemini-based multi-agent system that generates research hypotheses and ranks them in a tournament, with the survivors evolving over rounds. The scoring is self-judged, so the real test is downstream: several of its proposed drug-repurposing candidates for acute myeloid leukemia held up in vitro.

- **[Robin](/posts/20260606-robin-multi-agent-scientific-discovery/)** automates the full discovery loop, generating hypotheses, designing assays, and analyzing the wet-lab data that comes back, then re-hypothesizing for the next round, the step earlier systems left to people. Humans still run the experiments at the bench, and the system proposed and confirmed two drug candidates for dry macular degeneration.

- **[AI-driven formal proof search](/posts/20260606-ai-formal-proof-search/)** is the first large-scale test of AI generating machine-checkable proofs for open problems, closing 9 of 353 open Erdős problems in Lean. A plain generate-and-verify loop solved all nine on its own, while smaller models and the specialized prover alone solved nothing, which points to the frontier model rather than the orchestration as the source of the gains.

- **[An OpenAI model disproved a conjecture](/posts/20260606-model-disproves-discrete-geometry-conjecture/)** that had stood since 1946: a general-purpose reasoning model, not one built to prove theorems, settled a question in plane geometry by reaching into number theory, two fields with no obvious link. External mathematicians then had to check and make sense of the proof.

- **[Benchmarks in Leipzig](/posts/20260606-benchmarks-in-leipzig/)** had 49 mathematicians write 100 research-level questions with known answers to measure how good models really are. Counting one correct run in twenty as a solve, frontier models left only two unsolved, but many solves came on a single lucky run, so the headline number overstates how reliably the models answer.

- **[AI as a new scientific instrument](/posts/20260606-scientific-intuition-digital-speed/)** is the framing of a Google DeepMind essay, which casts AI as the latest lens after the telescope and microscope, supplying machine intuition across biology, materials, and mathematics while admitting that competition-style problem solving is not yet research and looking ahead to agents that generate their own hypotheses.

## What they share, and where they differ

A throughline that runs through all six is that AI is shifting from solving closed problems to taking part in open research, but in every case it still requires a trustworthy verifier, be it a Lean compiler, a wet-lab assay, a committee of mathematicians, or simply a known answer key. The formal route buys certainty but demands that someone formalize the problem first. The empirical route grounds claims in the lab but still needs people to run the experiments.

Where this goes next depends less on the models than on us. Generation and verification keep racing ahead, but digestion -- the slow human work of turning a verified result into understanding -- still lags, which is the [proof generation versus digestion](/posts/20260422-proof-generation-vs-digestion/) split Terence Tao named. Another open question is whether machine intuition can keep finding hidden structures where no one thought to look, or can only work where those structures were already there.
